synopsis: The booklet uses WorkSafe New Zealand for mines and quarries, WorkSafe Western Australia for autonomous-haulage incident reports, and HSE for Great Britain statistics; EU-OSHA is an information agency, not a regulator, used mainly for legislation summaries [f15673, f15674, f15681, f15685, f15686]. New Zealand's August 2017 alert documented heavy-plant interactions during ordinary operations, while its October–December 2019 event distribution was 46% overturning, 27% unintended movement or brake failure, 11% collision with other plant, 4% berm breach and 12% burst tyre; this single-quarter, incompletely reported distribution must not be treated as a long-term national profile [f3122, f15676, f15677, f15678, f3198, f3131]. WorkSafe WA's SIR 286 describes trucks resuming movement during recovery when communications returned, illustrating risks from misunderstood modes, overridden controls and desensitization; the booklet therefore calls for communications-loss, blocked-sensor, restart and recovery tests, although the original issue dates of SIR 226 and 286 remain uncertain despite March 2025 webpage dates [f15682, f15683, f15689, f15690, f11207]. HSE's cross-industry 2025/26 figures report 126 worker deaths, including 24 from moving vehicles, second to 31 falls-from-height deaths; its undated quarry guidance attributes 40% of accidents and 60% of deaths to transport, while cross-industry reversing guidance attributes nearly a quarter of workplace-transport deaths to reversing [f3146, f3147, f3155, f3156, f3153]. The 2024/25 figures require reconciliation: an HSE release attributes about 16% of fatal injuries to moving vehicles, whereas a vendor summary reports 14 of 124 deaths, a materially lower proportion [f3149, f3152]. The booklet found no EU-OSHA collision breakdown by movement type, and says non-EU target markets can make MSHA, WorkSafe WA and South African Regulation 8.10 the primary legal context [f15687, f11285].
